transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-12-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Dana Park (Redwood AE), Miguel Santos (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (CTO - Neoterra), Liam O'Rourke (ML Eng), Sofia Marin (Head Security), Arjun Patel (Infra)

Summary:
Priya and team are evaluating Redwood for model serving. Primary asks: open model comparisons (Llama-like vs Mistral-ish), context length up to 32k, multilingual performance (EN/ES/PT/JA), tool-calling for internal DB and search, and hosting options (hosted vs dedicated vs private/VPC/on-prem). Security and cost predictability are top concerns.

Topics:
- Model families and quantization tradeoffs
- Context length implications on latency/cost
- Tool-calling and structured output support
- Hosting modes and networking/KMS constraints
- Pilot/benchmark next steps

Action items (also in metadata): see above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Dana: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Dana from Redwood, I'm the AE on this. With me is Miguel, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya: Hi Dana, thanks. Doing good, excited to chat. I'll let the team intro themselves quickly.
[00:12] Liam: Hey, Liam here, ML eng. We're prototyping a customer-facing summarization that's multi-lingual, also some tool calls to our internal product DB.
[00:20] Sofia: Hey all, Sofia, head of security. I'll be focused on data residency, KMS, SOC2 stuff.
[00:25] Arjun: Arjun on infra, we'll need to know networking, VPC peering options and on-prem viability.
[00:30] Miguel: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: we'll run through model choices, context length tradeoffs, tool-calling patterns, and then hosting modes. We'll leave time for Q&A and next steps. Sound ok?
[00:37] Priya: Yep, perfect.

[00:45] Miguel: To kick off, can you remind us expected traffic patterns and latency targets? Even rough numbers help.
[00:50] Priya: Sure — expect 40 to 80k tokens/day initially, mostly bursty around business hours. Latency target is sub 700ms for single-turn summaries, prefer 300-500ms if possible. We care about tail latency too.
[01:05] Miguel: Got it. And context lengths? You mentioned 32k earlier — do you need that for every request or only some cases?
[01:12] Liam: Mostly the longer context will be for legal docs and long transcripts. Maybe 10% of requests will need 32k, most are 4k to 8k.
[01:20] Dana: Good. That distribution is important for cost decisions — serving 32k every time is very different than occasional.

[01:30] Miguel: On models, high level: open families split into Llama-like (Llama2/variants), Mistral-class, and some instruction-tuned hybrids. Llama-like tends to have more quantization maturity and larger community ops for 4-bit/8-bit. Mistral tends to be competitive in cost/quality for many tasks. Also mention we can support Redwood-verified model profiles so you get predictable performance.
[01:50] Priya: Any specific recommendations given our mix of summarization and multilingual? We've seen variable performance in Spanish and Japanese on some models.
[01:58] Miguel: For multilingual, a model trained or fine-tuned with multilingual data helps — some Llama derivs plus specialized multilingual variants perform better in ES/PT. For Japanese you might need a model with some tokenization tweaks. We usually recommend doing a small eval set across the candidate models.
[02:15] Liam: Ok, yes we'll share sample prompts. How about tool-calling? We want model to be able to call our internal search and product DB securely.
[02:22] Miguel: Redwood supports structured tool-calling and function-like calls in the API. From a security standpoint, you can run the runtime in Hosted mode with outbound calls proxied through a VPC egress, or in Dedicated/Private where you keep call endpoints inside your network. Also important: we support signing traffic and passing short-lived credentials to the tool executor.
[02:44] Sofia: When you say Hosted with VPC egress, what's the model for KMS and key material? We prefer the customer to keep keys.
[02:50] Miguel: For Hosted we offer integration with your KMS via customer-managed keys in many cases, but there's a control-plane tradeoff — keys for storage/encryption can be customer-managed; the runtime may require ephemeral keys. For Private/on-prem you control all keys. We'll surface a KMS architecture diagram.

[03:10] Priya: Cost — can you ballpark cost difference between running 8k context on hosted vs dedicated?
[03:17] Dana: Ballpark, hosted has usage-based per-token pricing which is simple but variable. Dedicated is a reserved GPU capacity — higher fixed monthly but often lower per-token. If your 32k requests are rare, hosted might be cheaper initially. Miguel, do you want to add?
[03:31] Miguel: Yeah, also caching and KV-cache reuse matter. If you can reuse prefixes, cost per effective token goes down. Redwood Optimize can recommend batching and quantization strategies to reduce unit costs.

[03:45] Liam: Quantization — we're exploring 4-bit and int8. Can Redwood serve int8 on Dedicated? Any perf numbers?
[03:52] Miguel: Yes, Dedicated supports quantized binaries and we have kernel selection that favors int8/llm.int8 where supported. For latency, int8 can be a nice middle ground. 4-bit can be good for cost but may need more eval to ensure quality. We'll include estimated CPU/GPU perf curves in the follow-up.

[04:10] Arjun: Networking question — if we pick Private, what's the deployment model? VPC connector, customer control plane?
[04:16] Miguel: Private gives you the control plane in your account (or a customer-managed control plane) and the runtime can be deployed in your VPC or on-prem. We have options: VPC peering, private link, and an on-prem package for air-gapped setups. There are firewall rules and egress controls we can share.
[04:30] Sofia: For audits, do you provide audit logs for token-level access and tool calls? We need to show who invoked what and when.
[04:36] Dana: Yes — Console provides token-level breakdown, per-route logs, tracing hooks, and you can configure retention. For enterprise customers, extended retention and SIEM integration are available.

[04:50] Miguel: Quick note on fallback policies — we can route requests to smaller models when capacity or latency spikes, and Redwood supports automatic model variants fallback. That helps maintain availability during spikes.
[05:02] Priya: That sounds useful. But how transparent are quality regressions when you fallback? We need to be sure summaries don't collapse.
[05:09] Miguel: We tie rollouts to eval sets — you can attach prompt-quality tests and get alerts on regression. Also we can do canary decoys for subsets of traffic.

[05:20] Liam: Regarding tool-calling again, we have some internal APIs that only accept requests from internal IPs. If we're hosted, how do we keep those calls internal?
[05:28] Miguel: You can either put the tool executor in your VPC and use a private egress, or run the entire runtime in Dedicated/Private mode so tool calls never leave your network. Hosted with VPC egress is middle ground but requires peering and careful firewall rules.

[05:44] Sofia: Data retention — we don't want prompts saved in a vendor-managed dataset. Are we able to prevent retention and have logs deleted after X days?
[05:51] Dana: Yes — we have retention controls and can offer non-retention options for enterprise contracts. We'll note that in the security deep-dive.

[06:05] Priya: For the eval, we'd like to test three model candidates: a Llama-derivative 30-70B, a Mistral-like 20-40B, and a compact instruction-tuned model for low-latency. Can Redwood host all three and run A/Bs?
[06:18] Miguel: Absolutely. Redwood supports multiple model variants simultaneously. We can spin up instances on Dedicated or hosted endpoints and run A/B traffic split with per-model metrics.

[06:30] Liam: How do we measure per-token cost when models have different tokenization and subtoken counts?
[06:37] Miguel: Our console normalizes costs to tokens and helps break down per-model effective cost after accounting for tokenization differences. We'll produce sample spreadsheets in the follow-up.

[06:50] Arjun: Roughly how long to spin up dedicated capacity for testing?
[06:55] Dana: For small Dedicated pools it can be days to a week for provisioning if you need reserved GPUs; hosted endpoints are immediate. If you need Private/on-prem it's a longer procurement and deployment flow — maybe 4-6 weeks depending on approvals.

[07:10] Priya: Sounds reasonable. One more thing: Japanese summaries need accurate honorifics and date formats — any specific model recs?
[07:19] Miguel: We can test a Japanese-finetuned variant; some Llama derivs fine-tuned on JP corpora do well, but will include that in the eval.

[07:28] Sofia: On compliance — ISO and SOC2 are must-haves. Do you have SOC2 Type II and penetration test reports?
[07:34] Dana: We have SOC2 Type II and we can share the compliance pack and pen test summary under an NDA. We'll add that to the follow-up.

[07:45] Priya: Great, thanks. Let's talk about a small benchmark pilot. We'd like to run a day-long pilot that runs 8k and a handful of 32k prompts, measure latency, cost, and quality. How would that work?
[07:56] Miguel: Typical flow: you share prompt set, we run it on hosted endpoints first for speed, then optionally run on a small Dedicated pool if you want reserved performance. We'll provide a results sheet with latency percentiles, token counts, and cost estimate. If you require private networking we'll coordinate the network setup.

[08:18] Liam: Any limitations on streaming vs non-streaming for long contexts?
[08:22] Miguel: streaming is supported; for long contexts streaming helps perceived latency. But true per-token cost still accrues. We'll show options for KV/prefix caching to avoid re-sending static context.

[08:34] Priya: Okay, can Miguel and Dana put a suggested plan and milestone? We want a pilot by mid-December ideally.
[08:41] Dana: We'll propose a plan: 1) share prompts + languages (Neoterra) 2) Redwood runs hosted baseline within 48-72 hours 3) run dedicated pilot if needed 4) security call. We'll put dates in the follow-up.

[08:57] (cross talk)

[09:05] Miguel: Quick note on tooling: if you plan to do tool-calling to internal search, design for idempotency and operation-level auth — we can help with example patterns.
[09:16] Arjun: One last infra Q: GPU types for Dedicated? A100s? 80GB?
[09:21] Miguel: We can provision a mix — A100 80GB or H100 depending on region and availability. For 32k contexts we'd usually recommend 80GB-class GPUs for best KV cache fit. We'll include recommended hardware matrix.

[09:36] Priya: This is helpful. Any known pitfalls from customers who tried a hybrid approach?
[09:41] Miguel: Hybrid is common: hosted for general traffic, dedicated for steady-state or high-SLA flows, and private for regulated data. Pitfalls usually are around fallback testing and monitoring — if you don't have good eval sets, rollouts can cause quality regressions. Also network egress and KMS misconfigurations are common in initial set-up.

[09:58] Sofia: We'll need a clear runbook for on-call and incident response if the runtime is in our VPC.
[10:04] Dana: We'll draft a runbook and include roles/responsibilities in the pilot pack.

[10:12] Priya: OK let's recap and assign owners.
[10:15] Dana: Recap: Redwood to send pricing + architecture + compliance pack; Redwood to run initial hosted baseline on 3 candidate models once prompts are received; Neoterra to provide prompt set and languages; schedule security deep-dive.
[10:30] Priya: Sounds good. Any other questions?
[10:34] Liam: Not from me.
[10:36] Arjun: No.
[10:37] Sofia: I'll coordinate the security sync.

[10:40] Dana: Great, thanks all. We'll follow up with dates.
[10:44] Priya: Thanks, appreciate it.

[10:48] (meeting ends)
